paras: The lynching ruse against William Miller took place at the jail in Aberdeen, Mississippi, on the night of December 24, 1881, when Miller, a Black prisoner held as accomplice in a triple murder, was taken from his cell "under the threat and pretext of being lynched." The removal left his cellmate, the white suspect W. Robert Jones, alone to be questioned, and Jones confessed. Both men were convicted at a special term of court in January 1882 and sentenced to hang.

Three sons of Judge J. P. Walker of Alabama, emigrants bound for Arkansas, were killed in their roadside camp about three miles from Aberdeen on the night of November 26, 1881. A Black man was soon jailed, and an Aberdeen dispatch of December 13 said he had told the story of the killings "after severe torture." When the Jackson Weekly Clarion printed the same dispatch, it said the confession came "after close questioning" instead.

Suspicion then fell on Jones, a white man from Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, who had traveled with the brothers. When his arrest was first reported, an Aberdeen correspondent wrote of "an infuriated populace" and the certainty of "Judge Lynch" if he were brought to town, and Sheriff Sykes telegraphed the arresting officer not to bring him there.

Detective Rush O. Bean nonetheless arrived in Aberdeen with Jones on the night of December 23, and Jones was placed in the same cell as Miller. According to the Appeal's Aberdeen correspondent, an eavesdropper overheard the two men discuss the crime, but "to make sure of the identity and guilt" Miller was taken from the jail the next night under a lynching threat that the dispatch called a "pretext." With Jones alone "in darkness and horror," two men questioned him until he gave a full confession. The dispatch does not name who removed Miller or say where he was taken.

On December 27 both men answered "I am guilty" in the committing court and were remanded to jail without bail. Their written confessions, made before Justice B. C. Sims, were printed by the Aberdeen Examiner, and Miller's, signed by mark, ended with the statement that it was made "without fear or compulsion."

At the special term on January 30, 1882, with Judge Green presiding, Jones pleaded guilty, while Miller pleaded not guilty and was convicted by a jury "after but a few minutes delay." Both were sentenced to be hanged on March 3, and no report of the execution appears in the coverage.

The lynching pretext appeared only in the Memphis Daily Appeal's special, headlined "At the Scene of His Crime," which reported it without comment, praised Bean and predicted the pair would "speedily be sent to the happy hunting grounds." Mississippi weeklies, among them the Jackson Clarion, the Greenville Times, the Pascagoula Democrat-Star and the Weekly Panola Star, ran short items identifying Miller as "the negro" or "colored" and forecasting the gallows, without mentioning the threat.

The Okolona Chickasaw Messenger called a formal trial "much better than Lynch law" while anticipating "a tight rope performance" near the banks of the "'Bigbee." Wire reports of the trial from Meridian ran in Dallas, Richmond and Savannah, identifying Miller only as "colored."

Accounts differ on how Miller's first confession was obtained: the Appeal's printing of the December 13 dispatch said "severe torture," the Clarion's printing of the same text said "close questioning," and Miller's signed statement disclaimed any compulsion.

bases: The one account of the act says the jailed Black prisoner was removed 'under the threat and pretext of being lynched' to isolate his cellmate; no violence beyond the threat is reported, apart from a separate claim that his earlier confession came 'after severe torture' (A6, A2).
Only the Appeal's Aberdeen special reports the lynching pretext (A6); other papers confirm Miller's arrest, confession and trial but not the threat (A7, A16).

accounts.label: Aberdeen special to the Memphis Appeal
accounts.gist: After eavesdropping on the shared cell, those handling the case took Miller from the jail 'under the threat and pretext of being lynched' so that two men could work on Jones alone, and Jones confessed.

accounts.label: Aberdeen dispatch on Miller's confession
accounts.gist: The Appeal's version says Miller told his story 'after severe torture'; the Jackson Clarion's printing of the same text says 'after close questioning'.

accounts.label: Miller's written confession

framing.detail: The Appeal's 'At the Scene of His Crime' special reported the lynching pretext as a detective's tactic, praising Bean and predicting both men would 'speedily be sent to the happy hunting grounds'.
Mississippi weeklies ran short items on the confessions and predicted hanging ('Their prospects for the gallows are flattering'), without mentioning the threat.
The Okolona Chickasaw Messenger called a formal trial 'much better than Lynch law' while joking about 'a tight rope performance'.
